title: Story of the Merchant Who Lost His Luck (தமிழ்)
summary: To illustrate his defense, Bakhtiyar recounted the history of an affluent merchant of Shiraz named Abu al-Majd: [TA]
keywords: story of the merchant who lost his luck
full_text:
To illustrate his defense, Bakhtiyar recounted the history of an affluent merchant of Shiraz named Abu al-Majd:

'Abu al-Majd had inherited a great fleet of trading ships, but within three years, misfortune struck his household with unceasing blows: three of his vessels were sunk by typhoons, his warehouses in Basra burned to the ground, and dishonest foreign agents absconded with his ledgers. He was reduced to absolute poverty, having to sell his furniture to purchase barley bread.

His companions mocked him, saying: "Your luck has died, Abu al-Majd; sit in the dust and beg!"

Abu al-Majd shook his head: "My gold has departed, but my hands can labor, my mind can calculate, and my honor is unbroken."

He took a job as a simple porter in the vegetable bazaar, carrying heavy baskets of onions and turnips for two copper coins a day. He performed his labor with such cheerful dignity, measuring his steps with care and never complaining, that the vegetable vendors entrusted him with the management of their collective scales.

Observing that much fresh produce spoiled during the summer heat, Abu al-Majd designed underground ventilated cooling chambers packed with mountain snow.

The merchants adopted his invention, and within five years, Abu al-Majd had revolutionized the storage of food across Shiraz!

The King of Persia appointed him Grand Controller of the Granaries, and his fortunes were restored threefold. He sat once more in his ancestral gardens, proving that misfortune is merely a shadow that vanishes before the steady light of honest labor.'
moral: Resilient labor and unyielding honesty turn repeated disasters into enduring prosperity. [TA]
